Primary motivation · Security skeptic

“Prevent automation from creating security gaps.”

The moment they start looking

A pre-release security gate/pen-test review flags an inconsistent policy evaluation outcome—one run denies, another allows—forcing an escalation before the app can ship.

What it costs them

Today the policy engine’s evaluation semantics are squishy—rules can fall through, resolve non-deterministically, or behave differently across environments. That’s how you end up with “automation did something weird” turning into an authorization gap: tool calls get allowed when they should hard-fail, and you can’t reconstruct the exact inputs, policy version, and resolution path that produced the decision. Net: you’re shipping insecure automation because you don’t have explicit deny-by-default behavior and provable decision provenance.

Job to be done Enforce deny-on-error and preserve decision provenance.
Measured on No security exceptions from agent decisions in audits.
Mandate Validate governance enforces deny-by-default and records decision provenance.
Biggest fear Undetected agent actions or silent policy gaps causing unsafe production writes.
Asks for this role None beyond the shared gaps on Page read.
Top pains
01 Undefined rule evaluation causing unsafe automation outcomes.
02 Decision provenance missing or unverifiable in audits.
03 Unclear data flows for agent decisions and logs.
Targeting phrases

deny by default agent approvals mobile −free

03 Unclear data residency and DPA — fix: DPA and data residency / retention statements

Primary motivation · The systems skeptic

“Avoid irreversible chain changes from automation.”

The moment they start looking

A policy change intended to unblock deployments is reviewed and someone realizes the draft would allow an unsafe contract deploy path because it wasn’t validated against known deploy request fixtures.

What it costs them

Your contract deploy pipeline is effectively running without regression tests for policy. There’s no reliable way to capture “this exact deploy request” as a golden test vector, and drafts can be saved even when they’d permit unsafe deployment paths. That’s how bad rules slip into the approval layer and the first time you learn about it is when a prod deploy is blocked—or worse, when an unsafe deployment gets through—because policy wasn’t validated against real transaction/deploy payloads up front.

Job to be done Validate policy drafts against saved real requests as test cases.
Measured on Zero production contract deployment incidents from automation.
Mandate Use saved requests as test cases and enforce pre-save validation.
Biggest fear An agent makes an unsafe production write without approvals or reproducible tests.
Asks for this role Show test-harness, saved-requests replay, and test cases.
Top pains
01 Agentic workflows performing risky production writes
02 No test-harness for saved agent requests
03 Slow or unverifiable human approvals for automated actions

Primary motivation · The pragmatic SRE

“Prevent outages from automated model operations.”

The moment they start looking

An automated retrain kicks off and starts emitting kubectl apply tool calls; the approval queue backs up and release engineering blocks on gated cluster changes.

What it costs them

Agent-driven automation is effectively operating as a privileged cluster operator. A retrain/redeploy workflow hits the cluster with kubectl apply and can roll workloads unintentionally—wrong namespace, wrong context, stale manifests—creating surprise rollouts and configuration drift. When things go sideways, you don’t just need “who clicked approve,” you need an immutable record of what the agent proposed, what was reviewed, and what was actually executed so you can do a defensible post-incident timeline.

Job to be done Pause risky agent tool calls for human approval before execution.
Measured on Zero unauthorized automated deployments to production.
Mandate Ensure human-in-loop approvals for agent-driven kubectl and retain frozen decision records.
Biggest fear Agents make production changes without clear human approval and no auditable record.
Asks for this role None beyond the shared gaps on Page read.

02 Approval queue grows and reviewers lack context to decide quickly.

What it costs them

Node-level actions (restart, cordon/drain, client resets) are not “just ops”—in a chain environment they can trigger cascading effects: validator churn, missed attestations, or outright chain reorg risk if done at the wrong time. If automation is taking these actions without an explicit human gate and a tamper-evident record of intent and context, you’re setting yourself up for self-inflicted downtime with no clean audit trail for incident review or stakeholder reporting.
